help_search_empty_hint: Try a shorter word, like “ping” or “loss”.
help_how_body: During the match, GameRoute spots the game server, traces the route to it, splits that route by operator and compares the ping with your usual ping on that server.
help_term_ping_desc: Round-trip time to the server, in milliseconds. When the server doesn't answer, GameRoute measures up to the last router that answers.
help_term_loss_desc: Share of probes left unanswered at a hop. GameRoute only counts it when it carries on to the last hop that answers.
help_term_jitter_desc: Gap between the fastest and the slowest probe to the same hop. The wider it is, the more uneven the ping.
help_term_hop_desc: A router on the route between your PC and the server. Hops are numbered in route order.
help_term_trace_desc: A measurement of the route to a server. Each probe goes one hop further than the one before, so routers answer one by one, with their ping.
help_term_at_least_desc: The server doesn't answer pings, so the measurement stops at the last router that answers, often at your ISP. The real ping is at least this value, and usually more.
help_term_silent_desc: The router forwards your traffic but doesn't answer probes. Many routers are set up this way; it's not an outage.
help_term_rate_limited_desc: The router limits its answers to pings to protect itself. That loss doesn't carry on to the next hops, so your match isn't affected.
help_term_problem_hop_desc: The router where loss of 10% or more, or unstable latency (a spread of at least 50 ms between probes), starts and carries on to the destination or the last hop that answers.
help_term_home_desc: Your PC and your local network, up to your router.
help_term_isp_desc: The first operator after your router: the one that provides your internet.
help_term_transit_desc: The operators between your ISP and the server's network. Your ISP chooses which ones your traffic goes through.
help_term_service_desc: The network that hosts the match server: the publisher's own, or its host's.
help_term_added_desc: The part of the ping added on an operator's network, according to the trace.
help_term_asn_desc: The number of a network on the internet, for example AS15557 for SFR. GameRoute reads it offline from GeoLite2 to name the operator of each router.
help_term_status_desc: With a usual ping, a match turns “{watch}” at +20 ms above it, “{degraded}” at +50 ms and “{critical}” at +100 ms. Without one, fixed thresholds apply to the ping. Loss that carries on to the last hop that answers is always compared with fixed thresholds. The match screen details the calculation under “{why}”.
help_term_usual_desc: Your usual ping to a server: the median of the last 20 measurements taken before the match at the same point, either the server itself or the same last router that answers. It takes at least 5. A “≥” value is never mixed with a real round trip.
help_term_unmeasured_desc: No router answered the trace, or no trace was run, for example for a server hosted on a CDN, which GameRoute doesn't trace. With no number, no threshold applies; it's not an outage.
help_term_session_desc: From the moment GameRoute detects a monitored game until it closes.
help_term_match_desc: The time the game spends exchanging with one game server. A session often holds several.
help_faq_at_least_q: Why does the ping start with “≥”?
help_faq_at_least_a: Riot servers don't answer any probe: Riot Direct, Riot's network, drops every packet that isn't part of a match in progress. When the server doesn't answer, GameRoute measures up to the last router that answers, often your ISP's, and puts “≥” before the value: the real ping is at least that value, and usually more.
help_faq_router_loss_q: Why can a router lose pings without it being a problem?
help_faq_router_loss_a: To protect their processor, many routers limit their answers to pings, or don't answer at all, while forwarding your traffic as usual. So GameRoute only counts loss that carries on to the last hop that answers. Otherwise the hop shows “{rateLimited}” or “{silent}”.
help_faq_measure_q: How does GameRoute measure a match?
help_faq_measure_a: A Windows service installed with GameRoute starts with your PC and runs pktmon, Windows' network capture tool. When a monitored game exchanges with a game server, GameRoute recognises it and traces the route to that server during the match, once per server and per session. Riot game servers are recognised from the first exchange; other games need 30 seconds of UDP traffic with the same address. The status then compares the ping with your usual ping on that server when there is one, with fixed thresholds otherwise, and persistent loss with fixed thresholds.
help_faq_isp_q: What should I send my ISP?
help_faq_isp_a: Open the session in question and choose “{copy}”. The copied text gives the verdict, the route by operator and the numbers for each match. Paste it into your message to support.
help_faq_add_game_q: My game isn't detected. What can I do?
help_faq_add_game_a: At startup, GameRoute looks for games installed with Steam, Epic and Riot. For another game, open the {games} screen and use “{add}” with its executable. To follow a program that's already open, use “{select}” next to “{start}” at the bottom of the sidebar.
help_faq_service_a: Capturing with pktmon and some of the probes need elevated rights. The capture service is installed with GameRoute, runs under the Windows system account and starts with your PC. The app itself runs without administrator rights. If it stops responding, a banner offers “{restart}”.
help_faq_anticheat_q: Does GameRoute touch the game or its anti-cheat?
help_faq_anticheat_a: GameRoute doesn't attach to the game process, doesn't read its memory and doesn't change any of its files. It spots the game in the list of running programs, watches network traffic at the Windows level with pktmon and sends its own probes along the route to the server. GameRoute isn't approved by Riot or any other publisher, so we can't guarantee how Vanguard or another anti-cheat will treat it.
help_faq_update_q: Can GameRoute update during a match?
help_faq_update_a: The update offered at startup waits until the monitored game is closed, then installs only if you agree. If you start it yourself from the {settings} screen during a match, GameRoute warns you that it will stop the measurement.
help_faq_data_a: Your sessions stay in a local database on this PC. GameRoute only connects to GitHub for updates, to Steam for game images and to CARTO for map tiles, and its traces send probes to your games' servers. Operators and countries are read offline from the GeoLite2 databases shipped with the app. There is no telemetry. Anonymous sharing, which you would turn on yourself, is planned for version 1.0; it doesn't exist yet.
help_data_attribution: Operators and countries: MaxMind GeoLite2 databases, read offline and updated with each GameRoute release. This product includes GeoLite2 data created by MaxMind, available from {url}, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

welcome_subtitle: Monitor your game network connections in real time.
welcome_admin_title: Why does it need admin privileges?
welcome_admin_body: Network packet capture (pktmon) and traceroute require elevated privileges. The capture service runs as a Windows service — you only see a UAC prompt at install time.
welcome_privacy_body: All session data is stored in a local SQLite database on your machine. Operators and locations of addresses are resolved offline with a bundled GeoLite2 database.
welcome_no_collection_body: No telemetry, no accounts, no cloud sync, no personal data collection. GameRoute only connects to GitHub for updates, Steam for game images and CARTO for map tiles.
welcome_launch_on_startup_description: Start GameRoute automatically when you log in, minimized to the system tray. You can change this later in Settings.
welcome_advanced_mode_description: Show technical details like protocols, hostnames, and packet counts. You can change this later in Settings.
service_warning_title: The capture service is not responding
service_warning_body: Some game connections will not be detected.
service_warning_fix_error: Could not restart the service. Try reinstalling the app or running it as administrator.
welcome_performance_body: GameRoute uses minimal CPU and bandwidth. Monitoring does not interfere with your games or streams.

settings_open_logs_description: Diagnostic files to attach to a bug report.
settings_capture_description: GameRoute relies on the “GameRoute Capture Service” Windows service, installed with the app. It starts with Windows and only passes the source and destination of packets to GameRoute, never their content.
settings_capture_feature_servers: The exact server of each match, even over UDP.
settings_capture_feature_voice: Voice chat measured apart from the game server.
settings_capture_feature_probes: UDP probes for servers that ignore pings.
settings_capture_stopped: Not responding. Without it, GameRoute can’t see game servers over UDP.
settings_local_description: No account, no cloud. Network operators are identified offline, with the GeoLite2 databases shipped with GameRoute.
settings_local_connections: GameRoute only connects to GitHub for updates, Steam for game images and CARTO for map tiles.
settings_retention_description: At startup, GameRoute deletes older sessions.
settings_retention_forever_description: Your sessions stay until you delete them.
settings_cache_description: Operator and country of each address, saved at capture time.
settings_wipe_description: Deletes every session, its measurements and the operator cache from this PC. Your settings and game list are kept.
